title: This Affordable Projector Has Pop-Out Surround Sound Speakers
gist: Wired's review of Soundcore's $299 Nebula P1i projector shows the brand pushing flagship pop-out-speaker hardware into a budget tier, while Google TV integration and battery-less design emerge as the key differentiators versus rivals like XGIMI and Anker's own MoGo 4.

insights.claim: Soundcore is extending the pop-out, positionable surround-speaker design from its flagship Nebula P1 and Nebula X1 Pro projectors down into a cheaper $299 Nebula P1i model, using premium-tier hardware features to differentiate a budget SKU rather than competing purely on price.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Watch for consumer-electronics brands using flagship-feature trickle-down into budget lines as a volume strategy in commoditizing hardware categories like portable projectors.
insights.quote: Apparently, bored by designing tiny can-sized projectors like the Nebula Capsule 3, the brand has become much more adventurous in their designs.
insights.locator: Soundcore has been having some fun lately

insights.claim: Built-in Google TV with QR-code smartphone setup has replaced manual Wi-Fi and streaming-app password entry in portable projectors, cutting first-use setup time to under five minutes and becoming a major usability differentiator in the category.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Projector vendors bundling Google TV/Android TV ecosystems gain an ease-of-use edge over proprietary-OS competitors, likely swaying purchase decisions in the sub-$400 segment.
insights.quote: Google TV has transformed the projector market.

insights.claim: At the sub-$300 price point, 1080p resolution paired with roughly 380 ANSI lumens brightness (and no 4K support) is standard across competing brands including XGIMI, BenQ, Samsung, and Aurzen, indicating 4K has not yet reached the budget portable-projector tier.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: 4K remains a premium-tier feature in projectors; expect it to stay absent from budget models until underlying display-chip and light-source costs fall further.
insights.quote: Some might me miffed the projector doesn’t support 4K, but at this price, the industry isn’t there yet.

insights.claim: The Nebula P1i lacks a built-in battery, which is its clearest competitive weakness against the $250 battery-powered XGIMI Vibe One and the $399 MoGo 4 (2.5-hour battery, 450 ISO lumens), even though the P1i delivers noticeably better cinematic picture quality than the cheaper Vibe One.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: Portability (battery life) is becoming as strong a purchase driver as core picture/audio specs in compact projectors; battery-less models risk ceding share to portable-first competitors even when their image quality is superior.
insights.quote: it's quite and doesn't have an internal battery, which means it’s not as appealing as truly portable option.

insights.claim: The Nebula P1i's flip-out, rotatable speakers (90 degrees horizontal, 200 degrees vertical) deliver a genuine, testable improvement in directional sound versus embedded projector speakers, but overall audio stays thin on bass and turns unpleasantly loud when pushed past roughly 35 percent volume.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: A distinctive hardware feature (pop-out speakers) produces a measurable audio gain, but doesn't overcome the bass and volume-ceiling limits inherent to small projector speaker drivers.
insights.quote: Pushed beyond about 35 percent and it’s just loud, but not in a good way.

insights.claim: Wired scored the Soundcore Nebula P1i 6/10, framing it as a reasonable value pick for casual, budget-conscious movie nights rather than a serious home-theater or fully portable device, given its lack of battery and sub-4K, sub-daytime-bright specs.
insights.speaker: Chris Haslam
insights.so_what: The product's addressable market is price-sensitive casual users rather than enthusiasts, limiting its ability to command premium pricing or a long upgrade cycle.
